_comment: THE BOOTH KNOWS WHO THESE PEOPLE ARE.
Every line here is filled from `drivers.py`, never from the session, and
a category is only ever offered for a driver whose record supports it —
`drivers.CATEGORIES` is the gate. So no slot in this file can air empty
(LAW 5): if a driver has no titles, the champion lines are not candidates
for him at all rather than rendering 'chasing , and'.
SLOTS, and what each one already contains:
{drv}         'Ayrton Senna'
{team}        'McLaren'
{titles}      'a seven-time world champion'   — carries its own article
{ntitles}     'seven'
{next_title}  'an eighth'                     — carries its own article
{wins}        'twenty-eight wins' / 'one win' — carries its own number
{nwins}       'twenty-eight'
{note}        'in red for the first time in his career' — a CLAUSE
LAW 13: never write a determiner in front of one of these. 'a {titles}'
airs as 'a a seven-time world champion'. The article is in the slot.
LAW 14: every line stands alone. The bag can draw any of these first, so
nothing here may read as a follow-up to another line.
TENSE IS FIXED AND IT MATTERS. These numbers are what the driver brought
TO this season, so the past tense is 'came into this year with', never
'has won this year'. The booth must never appear to know how the user's
season is going — it does not, and season.py is the only thing that does.
A false claim about Senna breaks the illusion harder than silence does.
If you cannot write a line that is true for every driver the category can
select, do not write the line.

_comment_live: THE POOLS BELOW ARE A DIFFERENT ANIMAL FROM THE ONES ABOVE.
Everything above states HISTORY — what a driver brought to the season.
These four state a RUNNING TOTAL: the historical record plus what has
happened in the user's own career. Race as Hamilton, win three, and the
next one is his ninety-ninth. Win the championship as him and it is his
eighth. Win it as Mansell in 1988 and it is his first.
They are filled from `drivers.Standing`, never from `Driver`, and their
{nth_win}    'one hundred and sixth' — the win just taken
{this_title} 'an eighth' — the title just won, counting this one
{ntitles}    the total INCLUDING the one just won
The maths behind them belongs to season.py and is exact. A title is only
ever called settled when the remaining points are known (LAW 4), and
`just_won_title` compares the season against the season one round ago so
a championship decided at round eight is not announced again at nine.
AND THEY APPLY TO THE AI TOO. If Senna wins the title in your 1988
career that is a first world championship for Ayrton Senna, and it is the
biggest sentence this booth will say all season.

_comment_teams: WHAT HIS CAR IS LIKE THIS YEAR.
Reached through the DRIVER, because that is what the booth is looking at
— a car on track with a name attached. `drivers.Team` is bound to each
driver at load, and the categories are refused unless the clause exists,
so no slot here can air empty.
{strength}  'straight-line speed — that power unit is the best on the
grid'  — a CLAUSE, present tense, no leading article
{weakness}  'a low-rake car that lost more than most to this year's
{tnote}     a hand-written clause about the team
These are the differences BETWEEN teams in one season and only exist for
seasons we hold. What the whole field is like — turbo lag, ground
effect, fuel rations — is `car_character` in booth_cars.json, which is
gated on era capability instead and therefore covers every car the user
owns, in a career or not.
CAPABILITY, NOT OUTCOME, exactly as in booth_cars.json: the booth may say
Mercedes have the straight-line speed and may not say who won the
constructors' championship. The user is driving this season.
